JSON: Name: jordan_party_legislation_effects Title: Mixed-methods causal evaluation of 2022 legislative reforms on the participation and accountability of Jordanian political parties Short Hypothesis: The 2022 constitutional and election/party law reforms causally increased measurable party effectiveness—operationalized as party vote share and seat share, district-level party coalition formation, and party internal accountability scores—relative to the 2011–2021 baseline. Related Work: Existing research documents links between legislative quality, electoral rules, and party performance and has used descriptive, comparative, and normative legal analyses to assess reforms in Jordan and comparable MENA states. Prior empirical work emphasizes correlations between electoral-system design and party representation, and case studies report that pre-2022 Jordanian legislation constrained party institutionalization. Comparative studies (e.g., Italy, Bahrain) highlight mechanisms by which improved legislative drafting and institutional design can change participation and oversight. Limitations in current work include heavy reliance on qualitative or single-election snapshots, lack of party-level longitudinal microdata analyses, weak causal identification strategies, sparse measurement of internal accountability (relying on anecdote or expert judgment), and limited exploration of district-level alliance mechanics. No prior study combines legal-text change mapping with party-level longitudinal causal inference (difference-in-differences, synthetic controls, interrupted time series) and primary survey measures of accountability across the 2011–2024 interval. Abstract: Problem: Jordan’s 2022 constitutional and election/party law amendments are hypothesized to alter political-party effectiveness via changes in legislative quality, participation, and accountability, but causal evidence is lacking. Approach: This study uses a mixed-methods pipeline combining legal-text coding of legislative quality, longitudinal party- and candidate-level administrative datasets (2011–2024), household and party membership surveys, elite interviews, and quasi-experimental causal inference (difference-in-differences, interrupted time series, and synthetic control). Main contribution: (1) a reproducible legal-change index tied to measurable electoral and organizational outcomes; (2) causal estimates of reform effects on party vote/seat shares, district-level alliance formation, and internal accountability indicators; (3) an integrated qualitative account explaining mechanisms behind measured effects. Expected outcome: precise estimates of the reforms’ impact on party performance and actionable diagnostics for where legislation still constrains participation or accountability, enabling targeted policy and research interventions. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Official election returns by candidate and district (parliamentary elections 2011, 2013, 2016, 2020, 2024); (2) candidate metadata (party affiliation, incumbency, demographics); (3) official party registration and membership records (2011–2024) where available; (4) Official Gazette texts of Constitution, Election Law, Party Law versions (pre- and post-2022); (5) nationally representative surveys on political participation, trust, and perceptions of party accountability collected in 2018, 2022, 2024 (or newly fielded panel); (6) NGO transparency/oversight indicators and WGI governance subindices 2011–2024. Baselines: pre-2022 period (2011–2021) and independent-candidate outcomes within Jordan; synthetic-control donor pool formed from comparable MENA countries without synchronous reforms. Primary empirical designs: 1) Difference-in-differences (DiD) comparing party-affiliated vs independent candidates before/after 2022 on outcomes: vote share, probability of winning seat, and margin of victory. Model: outcome_{i,t} = alpha + beta * post2022_t * party_affiliated_i + gamma_i + delta_t + X_{i,t}*theta + epsilon_{i,t}. 2) Interrupted time series (ITS) at national and district levels for aggregate party seat share and turnout. 3) Synthetic control using similar MENA polities to estimate counterfactual national-level party performance absent 2022 reforms. 4) Panel regression of party-level internal accountability score (survey-derived index combining disciplinary transparency, leadership turnover rate, grievance-resolution rate) on legal-quality index and controls, using party fixed effects. Controls and robustness: include district fixed effects, incumbency, economic controls (unemployment rate), and protest/region shock dummies. Instruments/Placebo tests: placebo reform years (2016, 2014) and permutation tests across districts. Ablation studies: A) remove constitutional-amendment component from legal-quality index to estimate marginal effect of election/party law; B) restrict DiD sample to single-member vs multi-member districts to test alliance mechanics; C) exclude parties below membership thresholds to test sensitivity to threshold rules. Evaluation metrics: average treatment effect on treated (DiD beta) with 95% CIs; change in national party seat share; change in party coalition formation rate at district level (% districts with joint party lists); change in internal accountability index (standardized effect size); placebo p-values from synthetic control. Statistical inference: clustered standard errors at district level, pre-trend tests, and sensitivity to omitted confounders (Rosenbaum bounds). Data preparation: legal texts coded into numeric indicators (clarity, participation provisions, accountability mechanisms) by two coders; inter-coder reliability reported. Risk Factors and Limitations: Data availability and quality: incomplete or non-standardized party membership and internal records; Official Gazette legal texts require interpretive coding introducing measurement error. Confounding and endogeneity: reforms may be endogenous to political pressures that also affect party outcomes (reverse causality); contemporaneous events (regional shocks, economic crises) may confound inference. Small-sample/time-series limits: limited number of national elections reduces statistical power for ITS and DiD; few comparable countries for synthetic control reduces donor-pool quality. Measurement bias: survey nonresponse and social desirability may bias accountability indices; party-affiliation coding ambiguity where informal alliances exist. Generalizability: findings specific to Jordanian institutional context and timing; mechanisms may not transfer to different electoral systems. Legal coding validity: mapping normative legal text changes to practical enforcement is imperfect; legal reform may not be implemented uniformly across districts. Causal-identification fragility: DiD requires parallel trends which may not hold; instruments for exogenous variation may be unavailable. Computational constraints: none critical, but complex synthetic-control and sensitivity analyses require careful tuning and may be sensitive to model choice.
